title: Gastric acid secretion: H2 blockers, PPIs and antimuscarinics
ariaLabel: Schematic of the parietal cell: histamine (H2 receptor), gastrin (CCK2 receptor) and acetylcholine (M3 receptor) all stimulate it, and the H+/K+ ATPase proton pump then secretes acid. H2 blockers and antimuscarinics block one input; proton pump inhibitors block the final common step.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lab value is shown or implied.
blockInfo: A drug of the chosen class acting at this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape). Less passes, so less acid is made. The proton pump is the last step of every route, so blocking it has the largest effect.

nodes.label: Histamine
nodes.info: Histamine released by enterochromaffin-like cells next to the parietal cells. It is the strongest local stimulus.

nodes.label: Gastrin
nodes.info: Gastrin released by G cells in the antrum when protein is eaten. It acts on parietal cells directly and by releasing histamine.

nodes.label: Acetylcholine
nodes.info: Acetylcholine from the vagus nerve, the cephalic and gastric phases of acid secretion.

nodes.label: Parietal cell stimulated
nodes.info: The parietal cell adds the signals from its three receptors: H2, CCK2 (gastrin) and M3 (acetylcholine). Histamine and gastrin act through cAMP and calcium and both end at the proton pump.

nodes.label: Gastric acid
nodes.info: Hydrochloric acid secreted into the stomach lumen.

edges.label: H2 receptor
edges.info: Histamine acting on the H2 receptor, which raises cAMP. H2 blockers occupy the receptor.

edges.label: CCK2 receptor
edges.info: Gastrin acting on the CCK2 receptor. No common drug blocks it.

edges.label: M3 receptor
edges.info: Acetylcholine acting on the M3 receptor. Antimuscarinics block it but also block M receptors elsewhere, so they are rarely used for acid.

edges.label: H⁺/K⁺ ATPase
edges.info: The proton pump in the parietal cell's secretory membrane exchanges H⁺ for K⁺. Proton pump inhibitors are activated by acid and bind it irreversibly, so every stimulus is blocked at the last step.

sources: The three signals and the pump. Histamine (H2), gastrin (CCK2) and acetylcholine (M3) all stimulate the parietal cell, and the H⁺/K⁺ ATPase is the final step; H2 blockers and antimuscarinics each block one input, and proton pump inhibitors bind the pump irreversibly. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Somatostatin and prostaglandin inhibition, the mucosal defence (mucus, bicarbonate), Helicobacter pylori, antacids and sucralfate, the delay and acid-activation of proton pump inhibitors (which are best taken before meals), rebound acid, nocturnal acid and the effect of long-term use are left out. The three inputs are drawn as equal in strength for teaching; real contributions vary. Levels and the size of each block are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
